_note: Step-by-step clues for Counting Figures (Chapter 31): the book questions and the past-paper questions filed under the chapter, by question id. Each list gives a way to count without missing any (by size, by the lines that make each shape, or one part of the figure at a time), gives the counts for the first sizes or parts, then sets up the total. The last clue never gives the answer. Questions marked needs-review have none. tools/check_clues.ts checks them.

cf-b01: Every triangle here has the top corner. So look at where the lines from the top cut the base, and the short cross line.
Along the base there are 4 small parts. Any run of parts next to each other makes a triangle: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10. The cross line has 3 parts: 1 + 2 + 3 = 6.
cf-b02: Count by size, smallest first, and write down each count so you don't count a shape twice.
The lines cut the square into 8 small triangles. Two small ones along a side make a bigger triangle: 4 of those. Each diagonal cuts the square into two halves: 4 more.
cf-b03: The star has a small triangle at each of its 5 points.
Each of its 5 lines is also the long side of a bigger triangle: a point together with the part of the middle next to it.
cf-b04: The big triangle has 4 small triangles along each side. Count by size, and count the ones pointing up and pointing down separately.
Size 1: 10 up + 6 down = 16. Size 2: 6 up + 1 down = 7. Size 3: 3. Size 4: 1.
cf-b05: Count by size, smallest first, and write down each count so you don't count a shape twice.
A 4 × 4 grid has 16 squares of 1 × 1, 9 of 2 × 2, 4 of 3 × 3 and 1 of 4 × 4.
cf-b06: Count one part of the figure at a time: the squares over the corners, where they overlap, the big square, and the small square in the centre.
4 squares over the corners; 4 small squares where they overlap the big one; the big square with its 4 quarters (5); the centre square with its 4 quarters (5).
cf-b07: Count the straight squares and the tilted squares separately.
The middle square and its 4 quarters make 5. The tilted square joining the middles of its sides is 1, and the 4 tilted squares around it make 4.
cf-b08: Count every box whose four sides are all drawn, big ones as well as small ones.
The whole figure, the strip on the right, everything left of that strip, its top strip, the part under the top strip, and the 2 parts that part is cut into.
cf-b09: A rectangle is fixed by choosing 2 of the lines one way and 2 of the lines the other way. With k parts in a row there are 1 + 2 + … + k ways to choose.
Here there are 4 boxes in a row and 4 rows: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10 ways each way.
cf-b11: A rectangle is fixed by choosing 2 of the lines one way and 2 of the lines the other way. With k parts in a row there are 1 + 2 + … + k ways to choose.
Parallelograms work the same way. 3 parts along a row: 1 + 2 + 3 = 6. 2 rows: 1 + 2 = 3.
cf-b12: A rectangle is fixed by choosing 2 of the lines one way and 2 of the lines the other way. With k parts in a row there are 1 + 2 + … + k ways to choose.
Parallelograms work the same way. 3 parts along each row and 3 rows: 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 each way.
ka1920m-51: Count by size, smallest first, and write down each count so you don't count a shape twice.
A 4 × 4 grid has 16 squares of 1 × 1, 9 of 2 × 2, 4 of 3 × 3 and 1 of 4 × 4.
ka1920m-52: A straight line right across a circle through its centre (a diameter) cuts it into 2 semicircles; two diameters across each other make 4.
The 3 circles round the centre are cut by both lines: 3 × 4 = 12. The 6 small circles are cut by one line each: 6 × 2 = 12.
ka1920m-53: Five lines come down from the top. Any two of them make a triangle with the base.
With the base: any 2 of the 5 lines, 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10. The short line across meets only 3 of the lines: 2 + 1 = 3 more.
ka1920m-54: The lines run in three directions: flat, slanting one way, slanting the other way. A parallelogram needs two lines from one direction and two from another.
Slanting both ways: 3 × 3 = 9. Flat lines with each slant: 3 + 3 = 6.
ka21m-63: Count one quarter of the square at a time, then the triangles made of halves of the square.
Each quarter with small lines has 13 (9 small, the quarter itself, and 3 made of several parts). Each plain quarter has 1. The diagonals cut the square into halves: 4 more.
ka21m-64: Every two small triangles that share a side make a parallelogram; bigger ones are made of 4 small triangles.
8 are made of 2 small triangles. 4 are made of 4: two along the bottom row, and two slanting across both rows.
ka21m-65: A straight line right across a circle through its centre (a diameter) cuts it into 2 semicircles; two diameters across each other make 4.
A line from the centre to the edge only does not make semicircles. The big circle and the three small circles have one diameter each: 4 × 2 = 8. The two middle circles have two: 2 × 4 = 8.
ka21m-66: A rectangle is fixed by choosing 2 of the lines one way and 2 of the lines the other way. With k parts in a row there are 1 + 2 + … + k ways to choose.
Here there are 5 up-and-down lines (4 parts: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10 pairs) and 4 across lines (3 parts: 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 pairs).
ka23m-23: Count by size, smallest first, and write down each count so you don't count a shape twice.
Count the single boxes first. Then the rectangles made of 2 boxes next to each other, then 3, and so on up to the whole figure.
Add up all your counts. How many rectangles?
ka23m-24: Count the triangles and the squares separately. Only shapes with four equal sides and square corners are squares.
Count by size, smallest first, and write down each count so you don't count a shape twice.
How many triangles, and how many squares? Which option has both numbers?

The big circle cut by the line: 2. Above the line: 2 medium arcs and 2 small arcs. Below the line: 2 small arcs and 1 medium arc.
